concepts.title: Universal Glorification
concepts.coreInsight: All creation in the heavens and earth glorifies Allah, demonstrating that praise of the Creator is the natural state of existence.
concepts.whyItMatters: When you glorify Allah, you join the cosmic symphony of worship - aligning yourself with the fundamental purpose of all creation.
concepts.arabicHighlight: سَبَّحَ لِلَّهِ مَا فِى ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَمَا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: آسمانوں اور زمین میں ہر چیز اللہ کی تسبیح کرتی ہے، یہ ثابت کرتے ہوئے کہ خالق کی حمد وجود کی فطری حالت ہے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: جب آپ اللہ کی تسبیح کرتے ہیں، تو آپ عبادت کی کائناتی ہم آہنگی میں شامل ہوتے ہیں۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: كل ما في السماوات والأرض يسبح الله، مما يدل على أن الحمد للخالق هو الحالة الطبيعية للوجود.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: عندما تسبح الله، تنضم إلى سيمفونية العبادة الكونية.

concepts.title: Divine Might
concepts.coreInsight: Allah is Al-Aziz (The Mighty) and Al-Hakim (The Wise) - His power is absolute and His wisdom perfect in all decisions.
concepts.whyItMatters: In times of oppression or difficulty, remember that true power belongs to Allah alone, and His wisdom guides all events to their proper end.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: اللہ العزیز (زبردست) اور الحکیم (حکمت والا) ہے - اس کی طاقت مطلق ہے اور اس کی حکمت تمام فیصلوں میں کامل ہے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: ظلم یا مشکلات کے وقت یاد رکھیں کہ حقیقی طاقت صرف اللہ کی ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: الله العزيز والحكيم - قوته المطلقة وحكمته الكاملة في جميع القرارات.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: في أوقات الظلم أو الصعوبة، تذكر أن القوة الحقيقية لله وحده.

concepts.title: Creation's Purpose
concepts.coreInsight: The opening verse establishes that all existence has one unified purpose: glorification of Allah, whether through conscious choice or inherent nature.
concepts.whyItMatters: Understanding this gives your life profound meaning - you are part of a universal purpose, not wandering aimlessly.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: افتتاحی آیت یہ قائم کرتی ہے کہ تمام وجود کا ایک متحد مقصد ہے: اللہ کی تسبیح۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: اسے سمجھنا آپ کی زندگی کو گہرا معنی دیتا ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: تثبت الآية الافتتاحية أن كل الوجود له غرض واحد: تسبيح الله.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: فهم هذا يعطي حياتك معنى عميقاً.

1.layer4: Both Shia and Sunni exegetes agree on the fundamental meaning of this verse, recognizing it as an assertion of universal divine glorification and a preface to the surah's main narrative. However, there are nuanced differences in interpretation. Sunni scholars like Fakhr al-Din al-Razi in Mafatih al-Ghayb emphasize the grammatical precision of the past tense verb, interpreting it as indicating the certainty and completeness of creation's glorification. Ibn Kathir focuses on this verse as proof that all creation worships Allah, whether consciously or through its ordered existence. Shia scholars, while accepting these interpretations, place additional emphasis on the connection between divine attributes and the historical events about to be narrated. Tabatabai notes that the specific pairing of might and wisdom at the beginning of this surah signals that the victory over Banu Nadir was not merely political but a manifestation of divine attributes in human affairs. Both traditions recognize the verse's function as a theological foundation, but Shia tafsir particularly emphasizes how it sets the framework for understanding the spiritual dimensions of historical events. Scholars from both schools agree that this opening invites believers to adopt a God-conscious perspective when examining worldly affairs.
1.layer4_urdu: شیعہ اور سنی دونوں مفسرین اس آیت کے بنیادی معنی پر متفق ہیں، یعنی یہ کہ یہ آیت عالمگیر الہٰی تسبیح کا اعلان ہے اور سورت کے مرکزی بیانیے کا دیباچہ ہے۔ تاہم تفسیر میں کچھ باریک اختلافات موجود ہیں۔ سنی علماء جیسے فخر الدین رازی نے مفاتیح الغیب میں ماضی کے فعل کی نحوی دقت پر زور دیا ہے، اس کی تفسیر یہ کرتے ہوئے کہ یہ تخلیق کی تسبیح کے یقین اور کمال کو ظاہر کرتا ہے۔ ابن کثیر نے اس آیت کو اس بات کی دلیل کے طور پر پیش کیا کہ تمام مخلوقات اللہ کی عبادت کرتی ہیں، چاہے شعوری طور پر ہو یا اپنے منظم وجود کے ذریعے۔ شیعہ علماء ان تفاسیر کو قبول کرتے ہوئے الہٰی صفات اور بیان ہونے والے تاریخی واقعات کے درمیان تعلق پر مزید زور دیتے ہیں۔ طباطبائی نے نوٹ کیا کہ اس سورت کے آغاز میں قدرت اور حکمت کا خاص جوڑ یہ اشارہ دیتا ہے کہ بنو نضیر پر فتح محض سیاسی نہیں بلکہ انسانی معاملات میں الہٰی صفات کا اظہار تھی۔ دونوں روایات آیت کے علمِ الہٰی بنیاد کے فریضے کو تسلیم کرتی ہیں، لیکن شیعہ تفسیر خاص طور پر اس بات پر زور دیتی ہے کہ یہ آیت تاریخی واقعات کی روحانی جہتوں کو سمجھنے کا فریم ورک کس طرح فراہم کرتی ہے۔ دونوں مکاتب کے علماء اس بات پر متفق ہیں کہ یہ ابتدائیہ مومنوں کو دنیاوی معاملات کا جائزہ لیتے وقت خدا کے شعور پر مبنی نقطہ نظر اپنانے کی دعوت دیتا ہے۔
1.layer4_ar: يتَّفق علماء الشيعة والسنة في الفهم الجوهري لهذه الآية، معتبِرين إياها إعلاناً عن التسبيح الكوني الشامل وتمهيداً للسرد الرئيسي في السورة. ويُبيِّن الفخر الرازي في مفاتيح الغيب الدقة النحوية لاستخدام الفعل الماضي، مفسِّراً إياه بأنه يُفيد اليقين والثبوت في تسبيح المخلوقات لله. ويُركِّز ابن كثير على هذه الآية باعتبارها دليلاً على عبادة الكون كله لله، سواء بالإدراك الواعي أم بالوجود المنقاد. ويقبل علماء الشيعة هذه التفسيرات، غير أنهم يُولون عنايةً أكبر للصلة بين الصفات الإلهية والأحداث التاريخية المرويَّة في السورة. وعند الطباطبائي أن المقارنة بين العزَّة والحكمة في مفتتح السورة تُشير إلى أن النصر على بني النضير لم يكن شأناً سياسياً خالصاً بل كان تجلِّياً للصفات الإلهية في شؤون البشر. ويتَّفق التقليدان على أن الآية الافتتاحية تدعو المؤمن إلى تبنِّي المنظور الإيماني في قراءة الأحداث الدنيوية، وإن كانت التفاصيل التفسيرية في الربط بين الصفات الإلهية والتاريخ أكثر حضوراً في الكتابة الشيعية.
1.layer1: Surah Al-Hashr opens with a powerful declaration of universal glorification: everything in the heavens and the earth exalts Allah. The Arabic word used is 'sabbaha,' derived from the root S-B-H, which conveys the idea of declaring Allah free from every imperfection and deficiency. This opening reminds the reader that before diving into the narrative of a specific historical event, the Quran first grounds us in the reality of Allah's absolute sovereignty and perfection. The surah is Medinan and was revealed around the fourth year of the Hijra in connection with the expulsion of the Banu Nadir, a Jewish tribe residing near Madinah. The two divine names mentioned here, Al-Aziz (the Almighty) and Al-Hakim (the All-Wise), are deeply connected to what follows: the expulsion of Banu Nadir was an act of divine power carried out with perfect wisdom. For the believer, this verse is a call to constant awareness that every created thing — animate or inanimate, visible or invisible — is in a perpetual state of glorifying its Creator. This awareness should cultivate in us a deep sense of humility, since we are part of a vast universe entirely devoted to Allah's praise. Practically, a Muslim should strive to make his or her own glorification conscious and intentional, understanding that when we recite 'SubhanAllah' we are joining the chorus of all creation.
1.layer2: Imam Tabari, in his Jami al-Bayan, explains the opening formula of glorification found across several Medinan surahs (known collectively as the 'Musabbihat') as indicating the absolute purity and transcendence of Allah from all deficiency. The verb 'sabbaha' in the past tense is understood by scholars including Tabari to denote a continuous, uninterrupted glorification — creation never ceases in its exaltation of its Lord. Ibn Kathir, in his Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim, notes that this opening connects to the surah's central theme: just as creation submits to Allah in glorification, so too were the Banu Nadir made subject to His decree regardless of their strength and fortifications. Ibn Kathir draws on the authority of Ibn Abbas, who called this surah 'Surat Bani Nadir,' affirming that its revelation was directly linked to their expulsion. The name Al-Aziz (Almighty) points to Allah's irresistible power by which no fortress or tribal alliance can stand against His will. Al-Hakim (All-Wise) indicates that every divine decree, including the exile of a people, is embedded with wisdom that may not always be immediately apparent to human observers. The Jalalayn similarly comments that these two names serve as a prefatory establishment of divine authority before the surah recounts historical events that demonstrate both attributes in action.
1.layer3: Wahbah al-Zuhayli, in Al-Tafsir al-Munir, observes that the Musabbihat surahs — those opening with glorification — tend to address pivotal moments of divine intervention in human affairs, and Al-Hashr is the most historically detailed among them. He emphasizes that the pairing of Al-Aziz and Al-Hakim at the outset serves a rhetorical function: it pre-emptively frames the entire narrative that follows as an expression of both divine power and divine wisdom, countering any cynical or purely political reading of the Banu Nadir's expulsion. Sayyid Qutb, in Fi Zilal al-Quran, reflects at length on the spiritual significance of universal glorification, describing it as a 'cosmic symphony' in which every particle of existence participates. He argues that this opening is intended to align the reader's consciousness with the divine perspective before recounting a chapter of early Islamic history — so that events are seen not through the lens of tribal politics but through the lens of cosmic order. For contemporary Muslims, this verse invites a worldview in which scientific discovery, appreciation of nature, and historical reflection all become modes of recognizing Allah's glory. Ibn Uthaymeen's commentary stresses that the believer's voluntary tasbeeh should be not merely verbal but lived — every act of submission and every recognition of Allah's perfection is itself a form of glorification that joins the universal chorus described in this verse.

concepts.title: Divine Decree
concepts.coreInsight: Allah expelled the Banu Nadir from Medina without battle - His decree came from where they least expected, bypassing their fortresses entirely.
concepts.whyItMatters: No worldly power or fortress can protect against Allah's will. True security comes from faith, not material defenses.
concepts.arabicHighlight: فَأَتَىٰهُمُ ٱللَّهُ مِنْ حَيْثُ لَمْ يَحْتَسِبُوا۟
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: اللہ نے بنو نضیر کو بغیر جنگ کے مدینہ سے نکال دیا - اس کا فیصلہ وہاں سے آیا جہاں انہوں نے توقع نہیں کی تھی۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: کوئی دنیاوی طاقت یا قلعہ اللہ کی مرضی کے خلاف حفاظت نہیں کر سکتا۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: أخرج الله بني النضير من المدينة بدون معركة - جاء قضاؤه من حيث لم يحتسبوا.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: لا يمكن لأي قوة دنيوية أو حصن أن يحمي ضد إرادة الله.

concepts.title: Terror in Hearts
concepts.coreInsight: Allah cast terror into the hearts of the Banu Nadir, causing them to destroy their own homes - an internal defeat before any external battle.
concepts.whyItMatters: True defeat begins in the heart. When you oppose Allah, inner peace is replaced by fear and self-destruction.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: اللہ نے بنو نضیر کے دلوں میں خوف ڈال دیا، جس سے انہوں نے اپنے گھروں کو خود تباہ کر دیا۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: حقیقی شکست دل سے شروع ہوتی ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: ألقى الله الرعب في قلوب بني النضير، مما جعلهم يدمرون بيوتهم بأنفسهم.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: الهزيمة الحقيقية تبدأ في القلب.

concepts.title: Lesson for Insight
concepts.coreInsight: The verse ends with a call to 'people of vision' to take warning - true sight means learning from the fall of those who opposed Allah.
concepts.whyItMatters: History provides lessons. Those with spiritual insight recognize patterns of divine justice and avoid repeating others' mistakes.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: آیت 'اہل بصیرت' کو تنبیہ لینے کی دعوت کے ساتھ ختم ہوتی ہے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: تاریخ سبق فراہم کرتی ہے۔ روحانی بصیرت رکھنے والے الٰہی انصاف کے نمونے پہچانتے ہیں۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: تختتم الآية بدعوة 'أولي الأبصار' لأخذ العبرة.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: التاريخ يقدم دروساً. أصحاب البصيرة الروحية يتعرفون على أنماط العدالة الإلهية.

2.layer4: Both Shia and Sunni sources agree on the basic historical facts of Banu Nadir's expulsion, including their treaty violation and assassination plot against the Prophet. Sunni scholars like Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi provide similar historical accounts, emphasizing the miraculous nature of the victory and how Allah cast terror into the hearts of Banu Nadir despite their fortifications. However, there are some differences in emphasis. Sunni tafsir tends to focus more on the military and strategic aspects of the siege, while Shia tafsir, particularly in Al-Mizan, emphasizes the theological and eschatological dimensions, especially the significance of 'awwal al-hashr' as pointing to future gatherings. Both traditions agree that this event demonstrated Allah's protection of His Prophet and the Muslim community. Regarding the distribution of the spoils from Banu Nadir, there is general agreement that they were considered fay' (property acquired without battle) rather than ghanimah (war booty), though Shia sources particularly emphasize verse 7's distribution formula that includes 'those of kinship' (dhil qurba), understood in Shia tradition as referring specifically to the Prophet's family, the Ahlul Bayt. This interpretive difference regarding fay' distribution reflects broader theological distinctions about the status of the Prophet's household.
2.layer4_urdu: شیعہ اور سنی دونوں ذرائع بنو نضیر کی جلاوطنی کے بنیادی تاریخی حقائق پر متفق ہیں، جن میں ان کی معاہدے کی خلاف ورزی اور نبی کے خلاف قتل کی سازش شامل ہے۔ ابن کثیر اور قرطبی جیسے سنی علماء نے اسی طرح کے تاریخی بیانات دیے ہیں جن میں فتح کی معجزانہ نوعیت اور اس بات پر زور ہے کہ اللہ نے کس طرح ان کے قلعوں کے باوجود بنو نضیر کے دلوں میں دہشت ڈالی۔ تاہم زور دینے میں کچھ فرق ہیں۔ سنی تفسیر محاصرے کے عسکری اور حکمت عملی کے پہلوؤں پر زیادہ توجہ دیتی ہے، جبکہ شیعہ تفسیر خاص طور پر المیزان میں علمِ الہٰی اور آخرت کی جہتوں پر زور دیتی ہے، خاص طور پر 'اوّل الحشر' کی اہمیت پر جو مستقبل کے اجتماعات کی طرف اشارہ کرتی ہے۔ دونوں روایات اس بات پر متفق ہیں کہ اس واقعے نے نبی اکرم صلی اللہ علیہ وآلہ وسلم اور مسلم برادری کی حفاظت میں اللہ کی مدد کو ظاہر کیا۔ بنو نضیر کے مالِ غنیمت کی تقسیم کے بارے میں عام اتفاق ہے کہ یہ غنیمت کی بجائے فیء یعنی بغیر جنگ کے حاصل ہونے والی جائیداد تسلیم کیے گئے، تاہم شیعہ ذرائع خاص طور پر آیت ۷ کے تقسیم کے فارمولے پر زور دیتے ہیں جس میں 'ذوی القربیٰ' شامل ہیں، جنہیں شیعہ روایت میں نبی کے خاندان اہلِ بیت سے تعبیر کیا جاتا ہے۔ فیء کی تقسیم سے متعلق یہ تفسیری فرق نبی کے خاندان کی حیثیت کے بارے میں وسیع تر علمِ الہٰی امتیازات کی عکاسی کرتا ہے۔
2.layer4_ar: يتَّفق مصدر الشيعة والسنة على الحقائق التاريخية الأساسية لإجلاء بني النضير، شاملةً نقض عهدهم ومؤامرتهم على اغتيال النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم. ويُقدِّم ابن كثير والقرطبي روايات تاريخية متشابهة، مُبرِّزَين الطابع المعجز للنصر وكيف ألقى الله الرعب في قلوب بني النضير رغم حصونهم. غير أن ثمة فوارق في التركيز: فالتفسير السني يُولي اهتماماً أكبر للجوانب العسكرية والاستراتيجية للحصار، في حين يُعنى التفسير الشيعي، ولا سيما في الميزان، بالأبعاد العقدية والأُخروية، خاصةً في دلالة «أول الحشر» على مراحل التجمُّع المستقبلية. ويتَّفق الفريقان على أن الحادثة دليلٌ على حماية الله لنبيِّه وللمجتمع المسلم. أما غنيمة بني النضير فمصنَّفةٌ بوجهٍ عام فيئاً لا غنيمةً في كلا التراثين، إلا أن المصادر الشيعية تُولي دلالة الآية السابعة في توزيع الفيء أهميةً بالغة، لا سيما في «ذي القربى» المفسَّرة عندها بالأسرة النبوية الكريمة، وهو اختلاف تفسيري يعكس الفوارق العقدية الأعمق في مكانة أهل البيت عليهم السلام.
2.layer1: This verse is the heart of the surah's historical narrative and contains the word 'al-hashr' (the gathering or exile) from which the surah takes its name. Allah informs us that it was He — directly and personally — who expelled the disbelieving People of the Scripture, specifically the Banu Nadir, from their homes at 'the first gathering.' The Banu Nadir had been a powerful Jewish tribe settled about two miles south of Madinah, with strong fortresses, date palm orchards, and long-standing alliances. Despite all this, they could not withstand the decree of Allah. The verse highlights the psychological dimension of their defeat: they had placed their trust in their fortifications, believing these walls would protect them from Allah's will. Yet Allah sent fear into their hearts from an unexpected direction. The phrase 'they destroyed their houses with their own hands' is a striking detail — in their stubborn refusal to let the Muslims inherit even the doorframes and timbers of their homes, they dismantled what they had built, unwittingly fulfilling the divine decree of ruin upon themselves. The closing exhortation, 'So take warning, O people of vision,' directly addresses believers of every generation: history is not merely a chronicle of events, it is a source of moral and spiritual lessons for those willing to reflect.
2.layer2: Tabari's Jami al-Bayan provides extensive detail on the historical background of this verse. Following the Prophet's migration to Madinah, a treaty was concluded with the Jewish tribes, including Banu Nadir. The occasion for the siege came when the Prophet visited Banu Nadir to request their contribution toward blood money for two men mistakenly killed by Amr ibn Umayyah al-Damri. During this visit, Banu Nadir plotted to assassinate the Prophet by dropping a boulder from a rooftop. Allah informed the Prophet of the plot through revelation, and he departed before it could be carried out. He then sent a message demanding their departure within ten days, but their chief Huyayy ibn Akhtab refused, emboldened by false promises of support from the hypocrites of Madinah led by Abdullah ibn Ubayy. The Muslims laid siege for approximately fifteen days — some narrations say ten, others twenty — before Banu Nadir capitulated and accepted exile. Ibn Kathir, drawing on hadith recorded by Bukhari, specifies that 'the first exile' refers to their departure to Khaybar and Syria, while 'the last exile' would refer to their final expulsion by Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab from the Arabian Peninsula. Ibn Kathir also explains the phrase 'cast terror into their hearts' as a reference to the supernatural fear Allah placed in them, consistent with the well-known hadith in Sahih Bukhari where the Prophet says he was given victory through terror cast into the hearts of his enemies at a distance of a month's journey.
2.layer3: Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran describes this verse as one of the most vivid illustrations in the Quran of the principle that power and fortification mean nothing when Allah decrees otherwise. He reflects on the psychological portrait drawn by the verse: confidence in material strength, the shock of divine intervention, and the bitterness of self-destruction. Qutb emphasizes that the image of people demolishing their own homes with their own hands is a universal lesson in how human arrogance, when confronted by the irresistible will of God, turns upon itself. Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir notes the legal significance of this verse in relation to the institution of fay — property taken from enemies without open battle — which became a major point of jurisprudential discussion among the fuqaha. He also highlights the closing phrase 'fa-i'tabiru ya uli al-absar' (so take warning, O people of vision) as a direct Quranic instruction that history must be read with moral intentionality. For contemporary Muslims living in times of political and communal upheaval, this verse teaches that reliance on walls — whether literal or figurative, whether military alliances or economic leverage — without alignment with divine guidance is ultimately self-defeating. The lesson is not triumphalism but rather a sober reminder that communities and nations rise or fall according to their faithfulness to truth and justice.

3.layer4: Both Shia and Sunni exegetes agree that this verse explains why Banu Nadir were exiled rather than executed despite their grave crime of attempting to assassinate the Prophet. Sunni scholars like al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir emphasize that the exile was itself a form of divine punishment and a warning to others who might consider treaty violation. Both traditions agree on the two-fold punishment structure: worldly exile and eternal Fire for those who died as disbelievers. However, there are subtle differences in emphasis. Sunni tafsir tends to focus more on the legal permissibility of either option (exile or execution) and the Prophet's choice to show mercy. Shia tafsir, particularly in Al-Mizan, places greater emphasis on the theological dimensions of divine decree and wisdom, analyzing why Allah specifically chose this particular outcome. Tabatabai's analysis explores the purposes served by exile rather than execution, including its function as a test for both Banu Nadir and the Muslim community, and its demonstration of Islamic principles of proportionality and mercy even toward enemies. Both traditions use this verse to teach about divine justice spanning two realms, though Shia scholars particularly emphasize the eschatological dimension and the principle that ultimate justice is realized in the Hereafter, which resonates with broader Shia theological emphasis on the Day of Judgment.

3.layer4_ar: يتَّفق علماء الشيعة والسنة على أن هذه الآية تُفسِّر لماذا آثر الله الإجلاء على الإعدام رغم جسامة جريمة بني النضير في محاولة اغتيال النبي. ويُؤكِّد الطبري وابن كثير أن الإجلاء كان عقوبةً إلهية بذاته وتحذيراً لسائر القبائل. ويتَّفق التقليدان على ازدواج العقوبة: إجلاءٌ دنيوي وعذابٌ أُخروي لمن ماتوا على الكفر. غير أن ثمة فوارق في التركيز: فالتفسير السني يهتمُّ أكثر بالجواز القانوني لكلٍّ من الخيارين وباختيار النبي الرحمة. أما التفسير الشيعي، ولا سيما في الميزان، فيُعمِّق في الأبعاد العقدية للقضاء الإلهي وحكمته، محلِّلاً لماذا اختار الله هذه النتيجة بالذات. ويستكشف الطباطبائي المقاصد المتحقِّقة بالإجلاء دون الإعدام، من بينها أنه كان اختباراً لبني النضير والمجتمع المسلم معاً، وتجسيداً لمبادئ التناسب والرحمة حتى مع الأعداء. ويستخدم الفريقان هذه الآية للتعليم بأن العدل الإلهي يمتدُّ على مساحة عالمين، مع ميل أوسع في الكتابة الشيعية إلى إبراز البُعد الأُخروي والتأكيد على المساءلة الكاملة يوم القيامة.
3.layer1: Having described the expulsion of Banu Nadir, Allah now clarifies a mercy embedded within that decree: had He not ordained exile as their punishment, He would have inflicted an even more severe punishment upon them in this world. The verse thus reveals a dimension of divine mercy even within what appears to be a severe judgment. The Banu Nadir were guilty of treachery — specifically of plotting to assassinate the Prophet of Allah in violation of their treaty. In divine justice, such a crime could warrant total physical destruction. Yet Allah chose exile over annihilation, preserving their lives and allowing them to depart with their possessions except for weapons of war. This restraint was not weakness but wisdom. For believers, this verse teaches that apparent hardship may often be a merciful alternative to something far worse. The second part of the verse, however, closes any door of complacency: the punishment of the Fire awaits them in the Hereafter unless they repent and embrace truth. This pairing of worldly mercy with the warning of eternal punishment reflects a recurring Quranic pattern — Allah's generosity in this life does not guarantee salvation in the next. Every person who encounters hardship should reflect on whether it might be Allah's gentle correction rather than His full wrath, and use that opportunity for repentance and return.
3.layer2: Ibn Kathir explains in his tafsir that this verse carries a hidden mercy that illustrates Allah's justice and forbearance simultaneously. Had direct physical punishment been decreed for Banu Nadir in the world, it would have come in the form of being killed on the spot, as happened to Banu Qurayza after their greater betrayal during the Battle of the Trench. Allah instead prescribed exile — a painful humiliation but one that preserved their lives. Tabari notes that some of the Companions initially expected the Banu Nadir to be fought and killed outright due to the gravity of their treachery, but the divine decree of exile was revealed as a distinct and lesser punishment that still served as a warning to all disbelievers. The verse also reinforces a fundamental theological point affirmed by the Sunni mainstream (ahl al-sunnah): that everything that occurs, including the outcomes of battles and exiles, is by Allah's decree and not merely the result of human agency. The phrase 'wa-law la an kataba Allahu alayhim al-jalaa' (had it not been that Allah had decreed exile for them) confirms that this was not a contingent political outcome but a divinely scripted event. Al-Qurtubi in his Jami li-Ahkam al-Quran connects this verse to the broader principle that punishment in this world can serve as an expiation or a warning, while the true and final reckoning awaits in the Hereafter.
3.layer3: Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir draws an important theological and ethical observation from this verse: it demonstrates that divine punishment in the world is always calibrated and purposeful, not arbitrary. The exile of Banu Nadir was a minimum-necessary intervention — sufficient to remove a threat to the Muslim community and demonstrate divine justice, while still leaving open the door of potential guidance for those who witnessed it. Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran reflects on the layered mercy in this verse: even those who oppose truth and breach covenants are given a chance to reflect before the ultimate reckoning. He argues that this Quranic perspective should shape how Muslims understand both divine judgments in history and their own dealings with opponents — firmness in justice, but never cruelty beyond what is necessary. Contemporary scholars also note that this verse addresses a subtle form of spiritual blindness: when people experience reduced consequences for their actions, they may interpret it as divine approval rather than divine forbearance. The verse's explicit mention of the Fire as an ultimate consequence corrects this misreading. For Muslim communities today, this verse encourages a realistic and spiritually grounded assessment of historical and personal hardship — understanding that apparent relief from full punishment is a mercy inviting reflection and repentance, not a signal that all is well.

4.layer4: Both Shia and Sunni scholars agree that this verse explains the core reason for Banu Nadir's expulsion: their active opposition to Allah and His Messenger through treaty violation and assassination attempts. Sunni exegetes like Fakhr al-Din al-Razi emphasize that the verse establishes the Prophet's special status, such that opposing him is tantamount to opposing Allah. Ibn Kathir notes that this principle serves as a warning to all who might consider harming or opposing the Prophet or working against Islamic teachings. Both traditions agree that 'severe in punishment' refers to Allah's justice being executed with power and precision against those who deliberately oppose divine guidance. However, there are differences in how this principle is extended. Shia scholars, following the teachings of the Ahlul Bayt, emphasize that opposition to Allah and His Messenger includes opposition to those whom the Prophet designated as his successors and the continuing guides of the Ummah. This is supported by narrations where the Prophet said that opposing the Ahlul Bayt is opposing him, and opposing him is opposing Allah. Sunni scholars generally focus more on the historical context of opposing the Prophet during his lifetime. Both traditions use this verse to establish the serious consequences of opposing divine guidance, though Shia tradition extends this principle more explicitly to the institution of Imamah.

4.layer4_ar: يتَّفق علماء الشيعة والسنة على أن هذه الآية تُبيِّن السبب الجوهري لإجلاء بني النضير: عداؤهم النشط لله ورسوله الذي تجلَّى بنقض العهود ومحاولة الاغتيال. ويُقرُّ الفخر الرازي بأن الآية تُثبت للنبي مكانةً استثنائية بحيث تعادل معارضته معارضةَ الله. ويُشير ابن كثير إلى أن هذا المبدأ تحذيرٌ لكل من قد يُفكِّر في الإضرار بالنبي أو بالإسلام. ويتَّفق الفريقان على أن «شديد العقاب» يُشير إلى تنفيذ عدل الله بقوة ودقة في مواجهة من يعارضون الهداية الإلهية عمداً. غير أن ثمة خلافاً في تمديد هذا المبدأ: فعلماء الشيعة بتعاليم أهل البيت يُمدِّون معارضة الله ورسوله لتشمل معارضة خلفاء النبي الشرعيين وأئمة الهداية المعيَّنين، مستندين إلى حديث النبي الذي قال فيه إن معارضة أهل بيته معارضةٌ له ومعارضته معارضةٌ لله. أما السنة فيُركِّزون في الغالب على السياق التاريخي المتعلِّق بمعارضة النبي في حياته. ويستخدم التقليدان هذه الآية دليلاً على عواقب معارضة الهداية الإلهية، مع امتداد أوسع لهذا المبدأ في التراث الشيعي ليشمل مؤسسة الإمامة.
4.layer1: This short but weighty verse provides the explicit reason for everything described in verses two and three: 'That is because they opposed Allah and His Messenger. And whoever opposes Allah, then indeed, Allah is severe in penalty.' The word 'shaqqa' in Arabic, here translated as 'opposed,' literally means to split or cleave — it conveys a vivid image of one who takes a path that diverges from and ruptures the path of Allah and His Messenger. The Banu Nadir's transgression was not simply political maneuvering or tribal rivalry. It was a fundamental choice to place themselves in opposition to the divine command and prophetic mission that had been made clear to them. This verse generalizes beyond the specific case of Banu Nadir and delivers a universal principle: divine law applies equally to all. Whoever takes the path of opposition to Allah and His Messenger — regardless of lineage, scripture, wealth, or fortification — will face the consequences of that choice. For the Muslim believer, this verse serves as both a warning and a comfort: a warning against allowing personal interests or cultural loyalties to override adherence to divine guidance; and a comfort in knowing that the seeming power of those who oppose truth is ultimately hollow. Allah's penalty ('shadid al-iqab') is a phrase that appears multiple times in the Quran to reinforce that the consequences of opposing divine guidance are not merely political or social but eternal.
4.layer2: Ibn Kathir in Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim explains that the word 'shaqqa' (to oppose) in this context is drawn from the same root as 'shiqaq' (schism), denoting a deliberate and active rupture. Banu Nadir knew of the Prophet's message — they were People of the Scripture who had anticipated his coming based on descriptions in their own books — yet they chose enmity over recognition. This made their opposition particularly serious in the eyes of the classical scholars, since it was not born of ignorance but of willful rejection. Tabari notes that the phrase 'shaqqa Allaha wa-rasulahu' (opposed Allah and His Messenger) links the two as a unified authority: to oppose the Messenger is to oppose Allah Himself, since the Messenger conveys nothing other than divine revelation. This is a foundational Sunni theological position confirmed by numerous hadith and Quranic verses. Al-Qurtubi uses this verse in his legal discussions to reinforce that the punishment of exile or execution for those who breach their covenants with the Muslim state is not a human decision but a divinely mandated response to a specific category of treachery. The closing declaration — 'Allah is severe in penalty' — is not presented as threatening language but as a statement of cosmic justice: the moral order of the universe has a consequence-structure built into it by its Creator, and that structure is inexorable.
4.layer3: Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran meditates on the moral clarity of this verse, noting that the Quran does not obscure the reasons behind divine judgments. The cause-and-effect relationship is stated plainly: opposition to Allah and His Messenger brings divine penalty. Qutb emphasizes that this transparency is itself a mercy — it gives human beings the information needed to avoid the path of ruin. He also observes that the verse universalizes the principle beyond Banu Nadir: the warning applies to any group or nation, at any point in history, that positions itself in deliberate opposition to divine guidance. Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir points out the structural elegance of these opening verses, where verse two describes the historical event, verse three explains the mercy within the judgment, and verse four states the root cause — forming a complete moral narrative. For contemporary Muslims, this verse raises the question of what it means to 'oppose Allah and His Messenger' in modern contexts. Islamic scholars explain that this does not mean every disagreement or scholarly difference of opinion, but rather the willful rejection of clear divine commands and the active sabotage of the Muslim community's welfare. The severity of Allah's response, as described here, underscores the seriousness with which sincere commitment to divine guidance must be taken in every age.

5.layer4: Both Shia and Sunni scholars agree on the basic context and meaning of this verse: it was revealed to address concerns about cutting date palms during the siege of Banu Nadir and to clarify that this action was divinely permitted. Sunni exegetes like Ibn Kathir narrate that the companions themselves differed on this action, with some proceeding and others hesitating, until the verse resolved the matter. Al-Qurtubi emphasizes that the verse establishes a principle of military necessity allowing exceptions to general environmental protections. Both traditions use this verse to discuss the ethics of warfare and the balance between moral principles and strategic requirements. However, there are some differences in emphasis. Shia scholars, particularly in Al-Mizan, place greater emphasis on the psychological and spiritual dimensions of the action: it was meant to break the opponents' will and demonstrate divine support for the Prophet, not merely to cause economic damage. Shia tafsir also tends to emphasize the phrase 'by permission of Allah' as indicating the Prophet's special spiritual station and his actions being divinely guided. Both traditions agree that the verse refuted Banu Nadir's propaganda criticisms and reassured the Muslim community. Scholars from both schools use this verse when discussing Islamic warfare ethics, environmental principles in Islam, and the methodology of balancing general rules with contextual necessities under proper religious authority.

5.layer4_ar: يتَّفق علماء الشيعة والسنة في الفهم الأساسي لهذه الآية: نزلت لمعالجة الجدل حول قطع النخل أثناء حصار بني النضير وتُوضِّح أن هذا الفعل كان مأذوناً به. ويُورد ابن كثير روايات تُثبت أن الصحابة اختلفوا في ذلك بين مُضيٍّ ومُتحرِّجٍ حتى فصلت الآية في المسألة. ويُبرز القرطبي أن الآية تُقرِّر مبدأ الضرورة العسكرية الذي يُجيز الاستثناءات من قاعدة الحماية البيئية العامة. ويستشهد الفريقان بهذه الآية عند مناقشة أخلاقيات الحرب والمبادئ البيئية في الإسلام وأسلوب توازن الأصول مع مقتضيات السياق تحت مرجعية دينية رسمية. غير أن ثمة فوارق في التركيز: فعلماء الشيعة ولا سيما في الميزان يُعطون ثقلاً أكبر للأبعاد النفسية والروحية للفعل، مُؤكِّدين أنه كان يرمي إلى كسر مقاومة الخصم وإظهار التأييد الإلهي للنبي، لا إلى الإضرار الاقتصادي وحده. كما يُولي التفسير الشيعي أهميةً خاصة لعبارة «بإذن الله» دليلاً على المنزلة الروحية الاستثنائية للنبي وكون أفعاله مُوجَّهةً وحياً. ويتَّفق الفريقان على أن الآية دحضت دعاية بني النضير وطمأنت المجتمع المسلم، وكلاهما يستخدمها في البحث الفقهي المتعلِّق بأخلاقيات الحرب وتقييد الموارد الطبيعية والمنهجية الجمعية بين الأصل والاستثناء تحت السلطة الشرعية.
5.layer1: The fifth verse of Al-Hashr addresses a specific controversy that arose during the siege of Banu Nadir: the cutting down of their date palm trees. The Prophet ordered some palm trees to be cut or burned to weaken the tribe's defenses and hasten the siege, while leaving others standing. The Banu Nadir and the Madinah hypocrites used this as propaganda, accusing the Muslims of spreading corruption and wastefully destroying property. The Quran responds directly: whatever was cut and whatever was left standing was done by Allah's permission, with the specific purpose of disgracing the 'fasiqin' — those who persistently transgress divine boundaries. The verse implicitly validates the Prophet's military judgment as divinely sanctioned and silences the objection by attributing both decisions — to cut and not to cut — to Allah's wisdom. For everyday Muslims, this verse teaches several things: that military and political decisions made by the Prophet under divine guidance are not subject to ordinary peacetime rules; that the apparent inconsistency in cutting some trees but not others was not arbitrary but purposeful; and that accusations of hypocrisy against the Muslim community made by its enemies should be evaluated carefully rather than accepted at face value. The verse also introduces the concept that divine permission underlies all human action in a way that cannot be reduced to merely human calculation.
5.layer2: Tabari in Jami al-Bayan records multiple narrations about the controversy over the palm trees. When the Muslims began cutting the date palms of Banu Nadir to facilitate the siege, the hypocrites and the Banu Qurayza raised an outcry, citing what they claimed was the Prophet's own prohibition against cutting trees and killing animals in enemy territory. Some Muslims were also uncertain about the permissibility of the act. This verse was revealed to clarify that in this particular case, the cutting was divinely sanctioned as a means of humiliating those who had transgressed their covenant. Ibn Kathir in his tafsir adds that the Prophet had initially ordered specific trees to be burned and others to be cut, and it was this command — attributed to divine guidance — that the verse upholds. The word 'fasiqin' (defiantly disobedient) in this verse is significant: it is the strongest term used so far in this passage for the Banu Nadir, indicating those who have stepped fully outside the boundaries of obedience to Allah. Classical scholars used this verse as a basis for discussing the permissibility of destroying enemy property during warfare under specific conditions — a topic extensively analyzed in Islamic law (fiqh). Al-Qurtubi devotes considerable space in his Jami li-Ahkam al-Quran to examining when the destruction of enemy agricultural property is permitted in Sharia, with this verse as the primary Quranic proof text.
5.layer3: Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir provides a detailed discussion of the legal principles derived from this verse regarding warfare and the treatment of enemy property. He notes that the mainstream Sunni legal schools have used this verse, together with relevant hadith, to establish nuanced rules: property may be destroyed when it serves a legitimate military purpose and not merely out of spite or excess, and the Prophet's conduct in ordering some trees to be preserved shows that restraint remains the default even in warfare. Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran focuses on the spiritual dimension of the verse, arguing that it teaches Muslims to understand that their actions in service of divine guidance — when properly authorized — carry a divine dimension that elevates them above ordinary human calculation. He is careful to note that this does not mean any Muslim can claim divine sanction for destructive acts; rather, it applies specifically to acts carried out under the direct guidance of the Prophet. Contemporary scholars discussing this verse also engage with the broader question of proportionality in conflict, noting that Islamic law's grounding of military conduct in divine permission — not unrestricted human will — actually provides a moral framework that limits excess. For Muslims living in contexts of political and military conflict today, the verse's emphasis on 'permission of Allah' as the governing principle of action is both a constraint and a source of moral clarity.

6.layer4: Both Shia and Sunni scholars agree that this verse establishes the category of fay' as distinct from ghanimah and explains that the wealth from Banu Nadir fell into this category because it was obtained without conventional battle. Sunni exegetes like al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain the distinction between fay' and ghanimah similarly, noting that fay' comes through surrender, treaty, or jizya without military engagement. Both traditions agree that the verse emphasizes divine agency in this victory. However, there are significant differences regarding the implications for authority and distribution. Sunni scholars generally interpret this verse as establishing the Prophet's discretion in distributing fay' according to the public interest, with the next verse providing guidelines but leaving considerable flexibility to leadership. Shia scholars, particularly following Tabatabai's analysis in Al-Mizan, emphasize that this verse establishes divinely ordained categories and distribution rules that continue to apply after the Prophet's time, with implications for how the Imams as his rightful successors should handle such wealth. The phrase 'Allah gives His Messenger authority over whom He wills' is understood in Shia tradition as indicating divine appointment of authority, supporting the concept of Imamah. Both traditions use this verse in jurisprudential discussions about wealth distribution and authority, though with different conclusions regarding the extent of divinely specified rules versus human discretion.

6.layer4_ar: يتَّفق علماء الشيعة والسنة على أن هذه الآية تُقرِّر حكم الفيء باعتباره مغايراً للغنيمة، وتُعلِّل بأن ثروة بني النضير دخلت في هذا الصنف لخلوِّها من القتال الفعلي. ويُفسِّر المفسِّرون السنة كالطبري وابن كثير الفرق بين الفيء والغنيمة تفسيراً متقارباً، ملاحظين أن الفيء يأتي بالاستسلام أو المعاهدة أو الجزية دون مواجهة عسكرية. ويتَّفق التقليدان على أن الآية تُبرز الفاعلية الإلهية في هذا النصر. غير أن ثمة خلافاً جوهرياً في الاستنتاجات المتعلقة بالسلطة والتوزيع: يرى علماء السنة عموماً أن الآية تُثبت تقدير النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم في توزيع الفيء وفق المصلحة العامة مع مرونة واسعة للقيادة. في المقابل، يُؤكِّد علماء الشيعة استناداً إلى تحليل الطباطبائي في الميزان أن هذه الآية تُرسِّخ فئات ذات طابع إلهي وأحكام توزيع تظل سارية بعد النبي، وتنتقل إلى الأئمة بوصفهم خلفاءه الشرعيين. وعبارة «الله يُسلِّط رسوله على من يشاء» يُفهم منها في التقليد الشيعي الدلالة على التعيين الإلهي للسلطة، مما يُعزِّز مفهوم الإمامة. ويستدلُّ كلا التقليدين بهذه الآية في النقاشات الفقهية حول توزيع الثروة وطبيعة الولاية، وإن تباينت الاستنتاجات في مدى تحديد الشريعة لأحكامها أو تركها للاجتهاد البشري.
6.layer1: Verse 6 of Surah Al-Hashr establishes a foundational principle in Islamic law concerning fai, which refers to wealth and property that returns to the Muslim community from enemies without actual armed combat. The historical backdrop is the expulsion of Banu Nadir, a Jewish tribe of Madinah who had entered into a peace treaty with the Prophet but then plotted against him. When their treachery was exposed, the Prophet besieged their fortresses and they eventually departed without a battle being fought. This meant no horses were spurred and no camels were driven in military engagement. Allah clarifies here that because this wealth was not acquired through conventional warfare, it did not fall under the rules of ghanimah, the spoils of battle that must be divided among those who fought. Instead, it belonged entirely to the Messenger of Allah to distribute as he saw fit according to divine guidance. The phrase 'Allah gives authority to His messengers over whoever He wills' reminds believers that divine power operates beyond conventional military means. The verse closes with 'Allah is over all things competent,' reinforcing that victory and provision come ultimately from Allah. The practical lesson for Muslims is trust in divine providence, recognizing that earthly resources are ultimately in Allah's hands and that the Prophet's decisions regarding such wealth were guided by revelation.
6.layer2: Imam Tabari in his Jami al-Bayan records extensive narrations establishing that this verse was revealed specifically concerning the property of Banu Nadir. He cites the companion Umar ibn al-Khattab who stated that the wealth of Banu Nadir was pure fai given to the Messenger of Allah, since no cavalry or camelry was deployed against them. Ibn Kathir in his Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim confirms this, drawing on the hadith recorded in Sahih Bukhari and Muslim in which Umar explains: 'The Prophet used this wealth to provide for his family's annual needs and spent the remainder on weapons and horses for the sake of Allah.' The term afaa in Arabic derives from the root meaning 'to return,' signifying wealth that returns to the Muslim community as its rightful due. Classical scholars differentiated sharply between fai and ghanimah: ghanimah requires actual military engagement and is distributed with one-fifth going to Allah and His Messenger while four-fifths go to the fighters, whereas fai is exclusively at the disposal of the Prophet and later the Muslim state treasury. Ibn Kathir emphasizes that the clause 'Allah gives authority to His messengers' establishes that prophetic authority is divinely backed, and enemies who resist this authority are ultimately overmatched regardless of their worldly strength. The Salaf drew on this verse to understand that material outcomes of da'wah and governance belong to Allah's arrangement.
6.layer3: Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir provides a comprehensive juristic analysis of this verse, explaining that fai forms the basis of the Islamic treasury known as bayt al-mal, which is meant to serve the public interest of the Muslim community rather than enriching individual fighters. He notes that the wisdom behind giving the Prophet exclusive authority over fai was to prevent conflict among companions over distribution and to ensure that societal priorities were met. Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran reflects on the deeper spiritual dimension: that Allah's messengers conquer hearts and territories not merely through military might but through moral authority and divine support. He sees in this verse an affirmation that Islam's expansion is not reducible to human calculation. In contemporary application, scholars note that this verse provides the Quranic foundation for state wealth management, public finance, and the principle that community resources must serve broad social welfare rather than concentrated interests. The verse also addresses a timeless human tendency to measure success by visible material effort alone; it corrects this by insisting that divine agency operates beyond what hands can accomplish. Modern Islamic economists such as Muhammad Umar Chapra have drawn on the fai concept when constructing models of redistributive justice in Muslim-majority societies.

7.layer4: This verse is one of the most significant points of divergence between Shia and Sunni interpretation with profound historical and theological implications. Both traditions agree on the basic categories mentioned in the verse and the principle of preventing wealth concentration among the elite. However, there are crucial differences regarding 'dhil qurba.' Sunni exegetes generally interpret this phrase more broadly as the poor among the Prophet's relatives or as the Prophet's clan (Banu Hashim) in general, without emphasizing specific individuals or ongoing institutional rights. In contrast, Shia scholars, based on narrations from the Ahlul Bayt, interpret dhil qurba as referring specifically to the Prophet's immediate family, particularly Fatimah, Ali, Hasan, and Husayn, and by extension to the continuing line of Imams. This difference has enormous historical consequences regarding the Fadak dispute. Shia sources maintain that the Prophet granted Fadak to Fatimah during his lifetime based on this verse, while Sunni sources generally deny this occurred or interpret it differently. The Fadak dispute after the Prophet's death became symbolic of larger issues regarding the Ahlul Bayt's rights and status in the Muslim community. Both traditions agree that the verse's final command about obeying the Messenger is crucial, though they differ on what that obedience entails regarding the Prophet's family. These interpretive differences reflect fundamental theological distinctions between the two traditions regarding the status and rights of the Ahlul Bayt.

7.layer4_ar: تُعدُّ هذه الآية من أبرز مواضع الخلاف بين التفسير الشيعي والسني، ولها تداعيات تاريخية ولاهوتية عميقة. يتَّفق التقليدان على الأصناف الأساسية المذكورة في الآية وعلى مبدأ منع تمركز الثروة. لكن ثمة خلافاً جوهرياً حول «ذوي القربى»: يُفسِّرها علماء السنة عموماً تفسيراً أوسع يشمل فقراء أقارب النبي أو بني هاشم عامةً دون التركيز على أفراد بعينهم أو حقوق مؤسسية مستمرة. في المقابل، يُفسِّرها علماء الشيعة استناداً إلى روايات أهل البيت بأنها تعني آل بيت النبي الخاص، لا سيما فاطمة وعلي والحسن والحسين عليهم السلام، وبالتبعية خط الأئمة المتواصل. ولهذا الخلاف تبعاتٌ تاريخية هائلة تتعلق بقضية فدك: يُثبت المصدر الشيعي أن النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم أعطى فاطمة فدك خلال حياته تطبيقاً لهذه الآية، فيما تنفي المصادر السنية ذلك عموماً أو تُفسِّره تفسيراً مغايراً. وقد غدت قضية فدك رمزاً لمسائل أعمق تتعلق بحقوق أهل البيت ومكانتهم في المجتمع الإسلامي. يتَّفق التقليدان على أن الأمر الختامي بطاعة الرسول أمرٌ محوري، وإن اختلفا فيما تعنيه هذه الطاعة بشأن أسرة النبي. وتعكس هذه الاختلافات التفسيرية فوارق لاهوتية جذرية بين التقليدين حول مكانة أهل البيت وحقوقهم.
7.layer1: Verse 7 of Surah Al-Hashr is one of the most far-reaching legislative verses in the Quran because it establishes both the distribution of fai wealth and the supreme authority of the Prophet in all matters. Allah specifies that fai belongs to Allah, His Messenger, the near relatives of the Prophet (the Banu Hashim and Banu Muttalib), orphans, the poor, and the wayfarer. The phrase 'so that it will not be a perpetual distribution among the rich from among you' is a powerful statement of social justice, directly prohibiting the monopolization of wealth by a privileged class. Allah does not want the same circles of wealthy people to endlessly pass resources among themselves while the poor remain deprived. This principle has permanent relevance for how Muslim communities and states should handle public resources. The second half of the verse then issues the most comprehensive command in the Quran regarding prophetic authority: 'Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, abstain from it.' Classical scholars consider this an absolute command covering all aspects of life, religious and worldly alike. It is the foundational proof text for the binding authority of the Sunnah. The verse concludes with a warning: 'Fear Allah, for Allah is severe in punishment,' reminding that violations of these principles carry divine consequences.
7.layer2: Imam Tabari records that the five categories listed in this verse were affirmed by the companions as the rightful recipients of fai, with the Prophet distributing the wealth of Banu Nadir among the poor Muhajireen who had no land or income in Madinah, along with two Ansar companions who were in dire need. Ibn Kathir highlights the phrase 'kay la yakuna dawlatan bayn al-aghniya,' noting that the word dawlah in this context means a revolving cycle, and the verse therefore prohibits wealth from circulating only among the rich. He cites the great jurist al-Shafi'i who treated this verse as the definitive text on the distribution of fai. Regarding the command to obey the Messenger, Tabari and Ibn Kathir both cite extensive hadith showing that the companions understood this as absolute: Imam Ahmad recorded that Ibn Masud said the Prophet cursed men who plucked their eyebrows and women who tattooed, and when a woman challenged him, he replied with this very verse, demonstrating its universality. Qurtubi in Al-Jami li-Ahkam al-Quran discusses the legal implications for the heirs of the Prophet, exploring whether the near relatives mentioned here refers only to those of the Prophet's time or extends to all descendants of Banu Hashim. The scholarly consensus of the Salaf was that the Sunnah is a binding legislative source equivalent in authority to the Quran.
7.layer3: Wahbah al-Zuhayli devotes considerable attention in Al-Tafsir al-Munir to the redistributive justice principle embedded in this verse, arguing that it constitutes a Quranic prohibition against economic oligarchy. He connects it to the broader Islamic economic framework in which zakat, waqf, inheritance laws, and prohibition of riba all work together to prevent wealth concentration. Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran is particularly forceful here, describing this verse as laying down the ethical cornerstone of Islamic social order: that all community resources must circulate broadly and serve those most in need. He writes with characteristic eloquence that the verse speaks not just to seventh-century Madinah but to every era and society where wealth threatens to calcify among elites. Regarding the command to obey the Messenger, Ibn Uthaymeen in his lectures emphasizes that this verse closes the door on any attempt to accept the Quran while rejecting the Sunnah, since the command to follow the Prophet is itself Quranic. Contemporary scholars of usul al-fiqh cite this verse as the definitive Quranic proof for the sunnah's legislative authority alongside the Quran. In the modern world, this verse has been cited in discussions about progressive taxation, public trusts, endowment funds, and state responsibility to redistribute national wealth equitably rather than allowing it to concentrate in the hands of a political or commercial elite.

8.layer4: Both Shia and Sunni scholars agree that this verse praises the Muhajirun and establishes their entitlement to support from fay' wealth due to their sacrifices for Islam. Sunni exegetes like Ibn Kathir emphasize this verse as praise for the companions who migrated from Makkah, often citing it as evidence of their collective virtue and reliability. The phrase 'those are the truthful ones' is used in Sunni tradition to affirm the righteousness of the Muhajirun as a group. Shia scholars agree that the verse praises those Muhajirun who maintained their truthfulness and support for the Prophet throughout their lives, but emphasize that the verse describes their state at migration and does not guarantee that all individuals maintained this level of faith permanently. Tabatabai in Al-Mizan notes that the verse praises qualities and actions, and that continued praise depends on continued demonstration of these qualities. This reflects a broader Shia principle that companionship with the Prophet, while honorable, does not automatically grant permanent righteousness if later actions contradict earlier faith. Both traditions use this verse when discussing the virtue of sacrifice for faith, though Sunni tradition tends to extend this praise more broadly and permanently to the Muhajirun as a group, while Shia tradition emphasizes individual accountability and the possibility of later deviation from early righteousness.

8.layer4_ar: يتَّفق علماء الشيعة والسنة على أن هذه الآية تُثني على المهاجرين وتُثبت أحقِّيتهم بالدعم من الفيء جزاءً لتضحياتهم في سبيل الإسلام. ويُبرز علماء السنة كابن كثير هذه الآية بوصفها ثناءً على الصحابة الذين هاجروا من مكة، مستشهِّدين بها دليلاً على فضلهم وعدالتهم الجماعية. وعبارة «أُولئك هم الصادقون» وُظِّفت في التقليد السني تأكيداً لصلاح المهاجرين كجماعة. ويتَّفق العلماء الشيعة على أن الآية تُثني على المهاجرين الذين أبقوا إيمانهم وصدق نصرتهم طوال حياتهم، لكنهم يُؤكِّدون أن الآية تصف حالهم عند الهجرة ولا تضمن لكل فرد بقاء هذا المستوى من الإيمان إلى الأبد. ولاحظ الطباطبائي في الميزان أن الآية تُثني على صفات وأفعال، وأن استمرار الثناء مشروطٌ باستمرار إظهار تلك الصفات. وهذا يعكس مبدأً شيعياً راسخاً: أن الصحبة النبوية شرف عظيم لكنها لا تمنح صلاحاً أبدياً مضموناً إذا تناقضت الأفعال اللاحقة مع الإيمان الأول. ويُوظِّف التقليدان الآية في الحديث عن فضيلة التضحية في سبيل الإيمان، وإن ميل التقليد السني إلى تعميم هذا الثناء وتثبيته على المهاجرين جماعةً أوسع وأرسخ، في حين يُشدِّد التقليد الشيعي على المحاسبة الفردية وإمكانية الانحراف عن الصلاح الأول.
8.layer1: Verse 8 of Surah Al-Hashr introduces the first of three groups whom Allah honors as deserving recipients of the wealth discussed in the preceding verses. This group is the Muhajireen, the poor emigrants from Makkah who abandoned their homes, wealth, businesses, and families for the sake of their faith in Allah. The verse describes them with remarkable dignity: they were 'expelled from their homes and their properties,' emphasizing that they did not leave voluntarily but were driven out by the Quraysh. Their defining quality was that they sought 'bounty from Allah and His approval,' meaning their sacrifice was entirely for a spiritual purpose. They also 'supported Allah and His Messenger,' making them active participants in the mission of Islam rather than passive victims. Allah then crowns them with the title al-sadiqun, the truthful ones, meaning their deeds perfectly matched their words. When they said they believed, their sacrifice proved they meant it. This is a profound teaching about the nature of true faith: sincerity is demonstrated through sacrifice. The Muhajireen gave up everything material to hold onto what was immaterial, and Allah here vindicates them publicly and eternally. For Muslims in every age, this verse is an inspiration that losses endured in the path of Allah are recognized by Him and carry eternal honor.
8.layer2: Imam Tabari records numerous narrations establishing that this verse refers specifically to the poor Muhajireen who received shares of the Banu Nadir property because they lacked means of livelihood in Madinah. He notes that the Prophet initially settled the Ansar and Muhajireen together, with the Ansar sharing their homes and orchards, but after Banu Nadir's expulsion the Prophet was able to establish independent support for the Muhajireen. Ibn Kathir elaborates on the phrase 'seeking bounty from Allah and His approval,' noting that this dual purpose was praised by Allah because their hijra was not merely to escape hardship but was motivated by genuine spiritual seeking. He contrasts this with a hadith in Bukhari in which the Prophet warned that whoever makes hijra for worldly gain will only receive that gain and nothing more. The description of being expelled from homes and properties was understood by the Salaf as applying to those whose wealth was seized by the Quraysh when they left Makkah. Qurtubi discusses the legal principle that emerges here: that genuine religious sacrifice and demonstrated commitment to Islam establish a legitimate moral claim on community resources. Imam Ahmad and others of the Salaf considered the Muhajireen the highest rank among the companions precisely because of the completeness of their sacrifice, which this verse divinely certifies through the title al-sadiqun.
8.layer3: Sayyid Qutb's commentary on this verse in Fi Zilal al-Quran is among his most moving passages. He reflects that the Muhajireen left behind not just property but identity, social networks, ancestral homes, and the psychological comfort of familiar land, and that Allah honors this precisely because it shows the human soul overcoming its deepest attachments when obedience to Allah demands it. Qutb sees in al-sadiqun a comprehensive spiritual certificate: these were people whose inner and outer realities were aligned in total integrity. Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir draws out the social welfare dimension, observing that Allah establishing a right of the poor Muhajireen in fai wealth was a precedent for the Islamic state's obligation to care for displaced and destitute members of the community. This has obvious contemporary resonance for displaced Muslim populations and refugees. Ibn Uthaymeen in his commentary emphasizes that the title al-sadiqun is not just praise but a lesson: that one's claim to true faith is measured by one's willingness to sacrifice for it. Modern Islamic scholars apply this verse to discussions of sincerity in worship and action, arguing that the Muhajireen represent the highest human expression of tawakkul, complete reliance on Allah. Their willingness to lose everything worldly, trusting that Allah's bounty and pleasure would be sufficient, is the model for the believer in every circumstance of loss and testing.

9.layer4: Both Shia and Sunni scholars agree that this verse praises the Ansar for their exemplary hospitality and generosity toward the Muhajirun. Sunni exegetes like al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir provide numerous narrations about the Ansar's selfless acts, using this verse as evidence of their collective virtue and reliability, similar to how they treat the verse about the Muhajirun. Both traditions emphasize the concept of ithar (altruistic preference) as a high moral station that the Ansar exemplified. There is general agreement on the historical examples of the Ansar sharing their wealth and homes with the Muhajirun. However, as with the previous verse, there are differences in how this praise is understood to extend. Sunni tradition tends to interpret these verses as confirming the permanent righteousness and reliability of the Ansar as a group, using them as foundational evidence for the principle that all the companions are trustworthy transmitters and models. Shia tradition, while honoring the Ansar's sacrifices and many individuals among them who remained loyal to the Ahlul Bayt, emphasizes that the verse praises their actions and state at that particular time, and that individual accountability continues. Both traditions agree that the verse's spiritual teaching about overcoming stinginess is universally applicable. Scholars from both schools use this verse extensively when teaching about generosity, community solidarity, and the ethics of welcoming those in need.
9.layer4_urdu: شیعہ اور سنی دونوں علماء اس بات پر متفق ہیں کہ یہ آیت مہاجرین کے ساتھ انصار کی مثالی مہمان نوازی اور سخاوت کی تعریف کرتی ہے۔ طبری اور ابن کثیر جیسے سنی مفسرین نے انصار کی بے نفس عطاء کی متعدد روایات نقل کی ہیں اور اس آیت کو ان کی اجتماعی فضیلت اور اعتمادیت کی دلیل کے طور پر استعمال کیا ہے، اسی طرح جیسے وہ مہاجرین کے بارے میں آیت کے ساتھ کرتے ہیں۔ دونوں روایات 'ایثار' کے تصور یعنی ایثارانہ ترجیح کو اعلیٰ اخلاقی مرتبے کے طور پر تسلیم کرتی ہیں۔ انصار کے مہاجرین کے ساتھ اپنی دولت اور گھر بانٹنے کی تاریخی مثالوں پر عام اتفاق ہے۔ تاہم جیسا کہ پچھلی آیت کے ساتھ تھا، اس تعریف کو کس طرح آگے بڑھایا جائے اس میں فرق ہے۔ سنی روایت اس بیانیے کو صحابہ کی مجموعی تعریف کے اثبات کے طور پر تعبیر کرتی ہے اور انصار کو بطورِ گروہ قابلِ اعتماد راویوں اور نمونوں کے طور پر استعمال کرتی ہے۔ شیعہ روایت، انصار کی متعدد افراد کی جانب سے قربانیوں اور اہلِ بیت کے ساتھ وفاداری کا احترام کرتے ہوئے، اس بات پر زور دیتی ہے کہ آیت اس مخصوص وقت کی ان کی اعمال اور حالت کی تعریف کرتی ہے۔ دونوں روایات اس بات پر متفق ہیں کہ بخیلی پر قابو پانے کے بارے میں آیت کی روحانی تعلیم عالمگیر طور پر قابلِ اطلاق ہے۔ دونوں مکاتب کے علماء اس آیت کو سخاوت، برادری یکجہتی، اور ضرورت مندوں کا خیر مقدم کرنے کی اخلاقیات کی تعلیم دینے کے لیے بڑے پیمانے پر استعمال کرتے ہیں۔
9.layer4_ar: يتَّفق علماء الشيعة والسنة على أن هذه الآية تُثني على الأنصار لضيافتهم الاستثنائية وكرمهم نحو المهاجرين. ويُقدِّم علماء السنة كالطبري وابن كثير روايات تاريخية عديدة عن أفعال الأنصار التفانية، مُوظِّفين هذه الآية دليلاً على فضلهم الجماعي وثقتهم، تماماً كما يفعلون مع آية المهاجرين. ويتَّفق التقليدان على مفهوم الإيثار بوصفه مقاماً أخلاقياً رفيعاً مثَّله الأنصار. كما أن الأمثلة التاريخية على سخاء الأنصار في تقاسم مالهم وبيوتهم مع المهاجرين موضعُ اتِّفاق. غير أن ثمة خلافاً في كيفية تمديد هذا الثناء. يميل التقليد السني إلى تفسير هذه الآيات باعتبارها تُثبِّت صلاح الأنصار الدائم وموثوقيتهم بوصفهم رواةً وقدوةً جماعية. أما التقليد الشيعي فيُكرِّم تضحيات الأنصار ويُثمِّن الكثيرين منهم الذين أبقوا وفاءهم لأهل البيت، مع التشديد على أن الآية تُثني على حالهم في تلك اللحظة التاريخية ولا تمنح صلاحاً مطلقاً لكل فرد في كل ما لحق. ويتَّفق الجانبان على أن التعليم الروحي في الآية بشأن قهر الشحِّ ذو تطبيق عالمي. ويُوظِّف علماء كلا المدرستين هذه الآية في الحديث عن الكرم والتضامن المجتمعي وأخلاقيات استقبال المحتاجين.
9.layer1: Verse 9 of Surah Al-Hashr is universally regarded as one of the most beautiful verses in the Quran about brotherhood, generosity, and selflessness. It praises the Ansar, the Muslims of Madinah who received the emigrant Muslims from Makkah and opened their homes, hearts, and livelihoods to them. Allah says the Ansar 'love those who emigrated to them,' which is striking because it describes not just a single act of generosity but a disposition of genuine love. They feel 'no jealousy in their breasts for what the emigrants were given,' meaning they had no resentment when the Prophet distributed the Banu Nadir wealth primarily among the Muhajireen rather than including the Ansar. The culmination of the verse is the description of ithar, self-sacrifice: 'they give others preference over themselves even though they are in need.' This is the highest level of human generosity, giving to others at cost to oneself. The verse then records the divine principle: 'Whoever is saved from the greed of his own soul, those are the successful ones.' Shuh al-nafs, the greed or miserliness of the soul, is presented as a spiritual disease that blocks success both in this world and the next. The Ansar's conduct, therefore, is not just an admirable historical story but a map toward spiritual success, teaching every Muslim that expanding one's circle of concern beyond the self is the path to flourishing.
9.layer2: Imam Tabari records several reports about the circumstances surrounding this verse. One famous narration describes how when the Prophet announced the distribution of Banu Nadir property, he asked the Ansar if they were willing to let their emigrant brothers receive these properties and continue sharing homes with them or if they preferred the properties be divided among everyone. The Ansar unanimously chose to let the Muhajireen have the properties and to continue their hospitality, and this verse was revealed in their honor. Ibn Kathir in his Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim cites the hadith in Bukhari describing how an Ansar man, when hosting a Muhajir guest and having only enough food for one person, extinguished the lamp so the guest could eat in full while the host and his wife sat in darkness pretending to eat. This hadith is often cited by commentators as the living embodiment of the ithar described in this verse. Ibn Kathir also records that Umar ibn al-Khattab recited this verse and wept when he heard about acts of generosity among Muslims. Qurtubi discusses the phrase 'no jealousy in their chests,' noting that the word hajah used here refers to genuine need, meaning the Ansar were not merely well-off people being generous but were themselves in need. This doubles the moral weight of their sacrifice. The scholars of tazkiyah al-nafs, the purification of the soul, draw heavily on this verse as the Quranic foundation for the virtue of generosity.
9.layer3: Sayyid Qutb writes in Fi Zilal al-Quran that verse 9 depicts a moral transformation in human beings that ranks among the greatest achievements of the Quranic message. He argues that self-preference is the deepest instinct of human nature and that the Ansar, by voluntarily overriding it for the sake of brotherhood in faith, demonstrated a spiritual revolution that no political ideology has ever produced. Qutb connects this to his broader theme that Islam creates a new kind of human being defined not by tribe or blood but by shared faith and love for Allah. Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir explores the practical applications of ithar in Muslim community life, including in financial dealings, social priorities, and civic responsibility. He notes that contemporary Muslim societies that struggle with tribalism, economic competition, and social fragmentation would find profound guidance in this verse. Ibn Uthaymeen emphasizes the warning embedded in 'whoever is saved from the greed of his own soul' as a spiritual diagnostic tool: a Muslim should regularly examine whether love of wealth, status, or comfort is causing them to withhold from others. Modern Islamic psychologists and educators cite this verse when discussing the development of empathy and communal responsibility in Muslim youth. The concept of ithar has also been applied in discussions of charitable giving, volunteerism, and the ethics of resource sharing in Muslim institutions and organizations globally.

10.layer4: This verse is interpreted somewhat differently in Shia and Sunni traditions, particularly regarding what it implies about attitudes toward early Islamic history. Sunni scholars generally interpret this verse as requiring uncritical praise and respect for all companions, arguing that asking for forgiveness for them implies assuming their general righteousness and avoiding any criticism of their actions. This verse is often cited in Sunni tradition as prohibiting any negative criticism of companions. Shia scholars, while agreeing that the verse teaches respect and supplication for earlier believers, emphasize that praying for forgiveness implies acknowledging that people make mistakes and need forgiveness. Tabatabai notes that the verse characterizes ideal later believers by their attitude of supplication and freedom from resentment, but this does not require historical revisionism or ignoring well-documented injustices such as the violation of Fatimah's rights or the later conflicts during the early Caliphate. Shia tradition maintains that one can pray for forgiveness for earlier Muslims while also acknowledging their errors and learning from their mistakes. Both traditions agree that the verse prohibits harboring resentment and ill-will toward believers, though they differ on whether this extends to those companions who opposed the Ahlul Bayt after the Prophet's death. The verse establishes an important principle of maintaining spiritual connection across generations while allowing for different interpretations of how that principle applies to specific historical figures and events.
10.layer4_urdu: یہ آیت شیعہ اور سنی روایات میں کچھ مختلف طریقے سے تفسیر کی جاتی ہے، خاص طور پر ابتدائی اسلامی تاریخ کے بارے میں رویوں کے مضمرات کے حوالے سے۔ سنی علماء عام طور پر اس آیت کی تفسیر اس طرح کرتے ہیں کہ یہ تمام صحابہ کی تعریف اور احترام کا تقاضا کرتی ہے، یہ استدلال کرتے ہوئے کہ ان کے لیے مغفرت مانگنا ان کی عمومی نیکی کو تسلیم کرنے اور ان کے اعمال کی کوئی تنقید سے پرہیز کرنے کو مضمر کرتا ہے۔ یہ آیت سنی روایت میں اکثر صحابہ کی کسی بھی منفی تنقید کو ممنوع قرار دینے کی دلیل کے طور پر نقل کی جاتی ہے۔ شیعہ علماء، اس بات پر متفق ہوتے ہوئے کہ آیت احترام اور مغفرت کی دعا سکھاتی ہے، اس بات پر زور دیتے ہیں کہ ان کے لیے مغفرت مانگنے کا مطلب یہ ہے کہ لوگ غلطیاں کرتے ہیں اور انہیں مغفرت کی ضرورت ہے۔ طباطبائی نے نوٹ کیا کہ آیت مثالی بعد کے مومنوں کو ان کے دعا کے موقف اور کینے سے آزادی کی خصوصیت دیتی ہے، لیکن یہ تاریخی نظرثانی یا اچھی طرح سے دستاویز کردہ ناانصافیوں کو نظرانداز کرنے کا تقاضا نہیں کرتی۔ شیعہ روایت برقرار رکھتی ہے کہ پہلے مسلمانوں کے لیے دعا کرتے ہوئے ان کی غلطیوں کو بھی تسلیم کرنا اور ان سے سبق لینا ممکن ہے۔ دونوں روایات اس بات پر متفق ہیں کہ آیت مومنوں کے خلاف کینے اور بد دلی کو ممنوع قرار دیتی ہے، تاہم ان میں اختلاف ہے کہ یہ نبی کی وفات کے بعد اہلِ بیت کی مخالفت کرنے والے صحابہ تک کس طرح پھیلتی ہے۔
10.layer4_ar: يتفاوت تفسير هذه الآية بين التقليدين الشيعي والسني، لا سيما فيما يتعلق بما تستلزمه من مواقف حيال التاريخ الإسلامي المبكر. يرى علماء السنة عموماً أن الآية تستوجب توقيراً وثناءً غير مشروطَين على سائر الصحابة، ويحتجُّون بطلب المغفرة لهم بأنه يفترض صلاحهم العام ويمنع أي نقد لأفعالهم. وكثيراً ما يُستشهَد بهذه الآية في التقليد السني لاستبعاد أي انتقاد للصحابة. ويتَّفق علماء الشيعة على أن الآية تعلِّم الاحترام والدعاء للمسلمين السابقين، لكنهم يُؤكِّدون أن طلب المغفرة يفترض الإقرار بأن البشر يقعون في الخطأ ويحتاجون للمغفرة. ولاحظ الطباطبائي أن الآية تُعرِّف المؤمنين اللاحقين المثاليين بموقفهم الداعي وبسلامة قلوبهم من الغلِّ، غير أن ذلك لا يستلزم تزوير التاريخ أو إغفال المظالم الثابتة توثيقاً كقضية حقوق فاطمة عليها السلام أو ما جرى من أحداث في الخلافة الأولى. ويرى التقليد الشيعي أنه يمكن الجمع بين الدعاء للمسلمين الأوائل والإقرار بأخطائهم والتعلُّم منها. يتَّفق التقليدان على أن الآية تنهى عن اضطرام الحقد والغلِّ تجاه المؤمنين، وإن اختلفا في ما إذا كان هذا يمتد ليشمل الصحابة الذين عارضوا أهل البيت بعد وفاة النبي. وتُرسِّخ الآية مبدأً جوهرياً في صون الصلة الروحية بين الأجيال مع اتساع المجال لتفسيرات متباينة في تطبيقه على شخصيات وأحداث تاريخية بعينها.
10.layer1: Verse 10 of Surah Al-Hashr completes a remarkable trilogy of verses honoring three groups of believers. After praising the Muhajireen in verse 8 and the Ansar in verse 9, Allah now praises those who came after them, meaning all Muslims of subsequent generations until the Day of Judgment. The defining characteristic of this third group is their prayer: 'Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith.' This prayer contains three profound elements. First, it is an act of humility in which later Muslims acknowledge that earlier Muslims hold a status they recognize and honor. Second, it is an act of love for people they have never met, the companions of the Prophet. Third, it is a request that Allah cleanse their hearts of any rancor or ill will toward fellow believers. The phrase 'do not place in our hearts any rancor toward those who believe' addresses a real spiritual danger: that partisan loyalties, historical grievances, or intellectual disagreements can breed animosity among Muslims toward one another. Allah's answer is to teach believers to actively pray against this. The verse closes with 'You are the Most Gentle, the Most Merciful,' affirming that Allah responds to this prayer with tenderness and compassion. This verse establishes love for the companions as an act of worship and teaches that membership in the ummah requires an open heart free from sectarian hatred.
10.layer2: Imam Tabari records that this verse was understood by the Salaf to establish that all Muslims who come after the companions are beneficiaries of fai in principle and, more importantly, are spiritually connected to the companions through shared faith and obligatory love. Ibn Kathir cites this verse as one of the proofs that loving the companions of the Prophet is an obligatory religious duty. He records a saying of Imam Malik: 'Whoever harbors hatred for the companions of the Prophet has no share in the wealth of Muslims,' indicating how seriously the early scholars treated this command. Tabari records that Abdullah ibn Abbas said this verse encompasses every Muslim born until the Day of Resurrection, making the supplication contained in it a permanent duty of the entire ummah. Qurtubi in his Al-Jami li-Ahkam al-Quran discusses extensively that this verse is direct Quranic proof that love of the companions is obligatory, and that harboring grudges against them contradicts the Quranic command. He also notes that the verse connects the well-being of the community to the spiritual purity of its hearts, arguing that communal harmony depends on each individual striving to remove rancor. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi in Mafatih al-Ghayb analyzes the psychological dimension of the verse, explaining that ill will toward believers is a spiritual poison that corrupts one's own faith regardless of whether the targeted person is harmed.
10.layer3: Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir emphasizes that this verse establishes a continuous chain of spiritual solidarity across all generations of Muslims. The ummah is not merely a sociological category but a living community of hearts connected by shared faith and mutual supplication. He applies this to contemporary Muslim unity efforts, arguing that sectarian conflicts and inter-Muslim hostility directly contradict this Quranic teaching. Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran reads this verse as describing the ideal Muslim consciousness, one that is oriented toward the future while remaining anchored to and grateful for the past. He writes movingly that the prayer taught in this verse cultivates the spiritual generosity of spirit that is the opposite of the religious tribalism and factionalism that divides Muslim communities. Ibn Uthaymeen stresses in his commentary that the prayer for the companions is not a mere formality but a genuine act of faith, since loving those whom Allah and His Messenger love is itself an expression of one's love for Allah. He also highlights the practical wisdom of praying against rancor in one's own heart, since the verse recognizes that such feelings can arise involuntarily and that the believer must actively combat them through supplication. In the context of contemporary Muslim discourse, this verse is frequently cited as the Quranic basis for the Sunni commitment to honoring all companions and maintaining respect across theological traditions within Sunni Islam.
